extracted.intended_audience: MIT mathematics students preparing papers and presentations
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and tooling recommendations for writing mathematical papers (LaTeX) and preparing presentation slides (beamer), aimed at MIT students but generally applicable to math students and instructors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer LaTeX defaults; prioritize the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: LaTeX makes many choices for you, and usually they are made for good reasons (involving the pleasure and convenience of the reader, not you).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't reflexively read the manual to change margins, fonts, spacing, etc.; changing defaults to suit the author's taste is often a mistake because LaTeX's defaults are chosen for readability and convenience of the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use AMSLaTeX packages (amssymb, amsmath)
rubrics_metrics.description: The big changes [to LaTeX] are invoked by the amssymb and amsmath packages loaded at the top of the template below.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Load amssymb and amsmath in your document preamble to get improved mathematical typesetting and additional environments and commands; these are invoked in the provided template.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align families of related equations
rubrics_metrics.description: One most important point is that AMSLaTeX offers more and better options for aligning families of related equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use AMS environments (align, alignat, gathered, etc.) to present sequences of related equations clearly; proper alignment improves readability and helps the reader follow derivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the provided LaTeX paper template
rubrics_metrics.description: This is a LaTeX template that you are welcome to use for your papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start from the template rather than reinventing document class/settings; the page provides a template (and notes that running pdflatex on it produces an output file). Using a standard template reduces formatting mistakes and preserves sensible defaults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult canonical LaTeX and mathematical writing guides
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended resources include The Not So Short Introduction to LaTeX2e, Short Math Guide for LaTeX, PRACTICAL SUGGESTIONS FOR MATHEMATICAL WRITING by Bjorn Poonen, and A guide to writing mathematics by Dr. Kevin Lee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to these concise, authoritative guides for concrete rules, tips, and broader advice on both LaTeX usage and the craft of mathematical exposition; they contain many valuable tips beyond what's summarized on this page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a beamer template for slides
rubrics_metrics.description: For presentations, if you wish to use slides, then we suggest you make a beamer file using this template.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start from the provided beamer template and included graphics files; customize the theme name (e.g., replace 'Goettingen') rather than hacking layout details from scratch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose an appropriate beamer theme from the gallery
rubrics_metrics.description: The overall appearance of your presentation is governed by the theme; there is a gallery of possibilities. Once you have chosen one, insert its name in place of 'Goettingen' near the top of the template.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick a theme that fits the context/audience and stick to it; themes control navigation, headings, and visual consistency—use theme features (like persistent section headings) to help orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid putting too much information on each slide
rubrics_metrics.description: The most common problem with slide presentations is putting too much information on each slide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep slides concise so the audience listens to you rather than reading dense small-font text; dense slides lead to divided attention and poor comprehension (anti-pattern: slides filled with many small-font equations/paragraphs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't go too fast; match audience pace
rubrics_metrics.description: A related problem is going too fast. A nice feature of blackboard talks is that the speed you can write is not so different from the speed your classmates can understand. It's guaranteed that the speed you can click is much greater than the speed they can understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pace your presentation to the audience's ability to absorb material; avoid rapid slide advances and give time for processing. When possible, slow down or supplement slides with board work to control pace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep important definitions and notation visible
rubrics_metrics.description: A built-in disadvantage of slides ... is that it's difficult or impossible to leave important definitions and notation up where the audience can look back at them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigate by using some boards along with slides or choosing a beamer theme that shows persistent context (e.g., all section headings) on every slide; explicitly restate or display key definitions/notation when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer blackboard talks for natural pacing and retention when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: A nice feature of blackboard talks is that the speed you can write is not so different from the speed your classmates can understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider giving a blackboard talk (or mixing boards with slides) when you need to control pacing, allow the audience to follow derivations step-by-step, or leave material visible for longer than a slide allows.
